items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张九碟装合集系统回顾了金珍姬四十年的创作与即兴历程，既收录管弦乐和室内乐作品，也记录她与多位即兴演奏家的合作。她将韩国传统乐器玄琴接入电脑接口与信号处理，大幅拓展了这一古老乐器的声音边界。乐评提到，她在整理早期作品时感到惊讶，那些用西方乐器转写韩国音乐或使用图形记谱的尝试来自年轻无畏的自己。她也认识到玄琴音色有限，但具有冥想般的“空”与“慢”的能量，而她正是凭借这种内向能量与众多顶尖即兴乐手对话。整个合集近乎对半分配作曲与即兴，呈现出每一首作品都扎根韩国文化、同时又实现她赴美创作新音乐目标的脉络。对关注传统乐器当代化、跨文化即兴与实验声音的听众而言，这是一份有档案价值的聆听样本。

items.body: We are extremely excited about the Experimental segment of our Fall Music Preview, as it contains all manner of treasures! This fall’s releases include an album that concentrates on the metallic aspects of percussion and other works inspired by biomes, nest building and Haruki Murakami’s IQ84. The youngest performers are in the single digits, while the oldest is an octogenarian. With such a wide variety here on display, there’s something for everyone to enjoy. So set aside all expectations, put those earbuds in and prepare to be dazzled! Our cover image is a lovely collage designed by Sonnenzimmer for Katherine Young‘s BIOMES, covered below. Electroacoustic Lea Bertucci and Michael Beharie may be vying for attention with Sarah Davachi come year’s end, as Bow and Arrow walks through similar glens. Their sound, billed as “electroacoustic spectral folk,” puts one in mind of autumn and its mysterious natural timbres (NNA Tapes, October 23). Weston Olenki and TAK ensemble‘s when the great fires were lit on the other side of the ocean is one of the season’s most distinct recordings, inspired by the writings of W.G. Sebald on electricity and including field recordings from Tesla’s first power plant. The limited edition includes both the score and a lecture packet (Sweet Wreath, September 30). Hallow Ground offers John McCowen‘s Pressure Chords feat. Lucy Railton, Weston Olencki, an album that could just as easily landed in our Drone department. With contrabass clarinet, cello and trombone, the trio stretches tones taffy-thin before rebuilding them layer by layer (September 18). After this comes Jordan Sand‘s Baby Ghost, whose tendrils of falsetto voice are mingled with passages of bowed double bass, producing an otherworldly effect (October 2).   Free improvisation meets metal and drone on Mats Erlandsson & Gus Loxbo‘s Minnets Långa Kedjor (XKatedral, September 18), a moody album with narration from Maria W Horn. At times, the work invokes Swans, which makes sense as Michael Gira offers guest narration on Horn’s own album, Melting Pillars of Snow, out October 2 on the same label. Buy them both to experience the depths of a dark autumn.   Misanthropic Agenda‘s first releases of the season are out today. Vincent Grimaldi‘s Amorcie De Champ is crinkly and dark, a collage of field recordings, turntables and tapes, while the troublingly named Perverts in White Shirts offers “cringe pop” on the 28-track CULTrully appropriate songs and revisited memories (September 4). The creaks, rustles and cracks of Liths (Sarah Hennies, Willie B. and Keir Neuringer) make Ascending the Depths a perfect album for fall, when the shadows creep across the forest floor and strange creatures come out to play (Dinzu Artefacts, September 25).   Mark Peter Wright offers pure North Yorkshire field recordings on Field Crafting, interacting with his environment in a way that honors his surroundings while bringing them to life (Flaming Pines, October 8). Icelandic field recordings decorate the background of Marja Ahti & John McCowen‘s Errands, which fills in the spaces with recorder and clarinet (Black Truffle, September 25). Mixing field recordings with electro-acoustic elements, Crys Cole presents Testing the Waters, a single-track album whose rivers run deep (Persistence of Sound, October 9). Midway between minimalism and drone lies Roel Meelkop‘s Antithesis, a set sounds that relate to each other in interlocking ways (Crónica, September 8). CZN (copper, zinc and nickel) combines the work of percussionist-sculptor João Pais Filipe, composer-drummer Valentina Magaletti, and producer Leon Marks. The concentration on gongs, cymbals and other metal objects earns the trio its moniker, hearkening back to the work of mHz. Parallel Commutator is out October 16 on Oath.   Katherine Young‘s BIOMES is breathy and intense, initially inspired by lichen before expanding into wetlands, oyster reefs and more. Joining the artist: Olivia Block, Ben LaMar Gay, Brian Chase, Tim Daisy, and Yarn/Wire, who help to make the album a three-dimensional experience (Chaikin, September 18). We’re loving the sheets of rain in “Thunder Covered Brush,” the opening track of M. Sage‘s Brush Flier. The artist draws from multiple genres on this album, including ambient, folk and electronic, keeping the dynamic contrast high (RVNG Intl., September 25). ICMC: Best of the Listening Rooms is an electro-acoustic extravaganza, drawing from the 50th anniversary of the International Computer Music Conference. Featuring music from around the world, the compilation is as much a treat for the mind as it is the ears (Ravello, September 18). Yanick Soland is Walking on Rubber Eggshells. The set is a potpourri of sounds: flute, violin, zither, bowed koto and voice. Originally part of a solo exhibition, it displays the “come hither” sound that in person must have drawn people into the room (Futura Resistenza, September 28). Kaoru Watanabe‘s The Arch draws the listener deep into Japanese musical heritage, as the composer plays multiple instruments, including shinobue, ryuteki, hichiriki, taiko, atarigane, suzu, ame uchiwa, and koto, along with some instruments associated with the West. The songs tell stories, teach lessons, and entertain (New Amsterdam, September 18). Using “rage as a creative process,” Marina Herlop presents Dja Dja, which contains multiple nooks and crannies, featuring gamelan, voice and unconventional rhythms, and ultimately comes across as positive. There’s even a t-shirt bundle (October 9).   Jazz and Improvisation 577 Records always has its act together when it comes to pre-orders, which is why they get the lead-off spot. But this season, their first release is a true outlier. Released through the Positive Elevation imprint, the self-titled MY FACE IS DANCING is a family affair ~ specifically, the family of Federico Ughi, who records with his three sons. There’s hip-hop here alongside the jazz, and even some slam poetry: a photo album in sonic form (September 4). Two weeks later, Rafael Zaldivar | McBride | Mela release the languid Meeting in New York, Volume One, which was just recorded this past April (September 18). Savant Fleur follows with the raucous Hocketus, which indulges in dissonance, atonalism and noise, mangling the strings of the cello and violin (September 25). Then the attention turns to the solo work of Cuban musician Francesco Mela, playing multiple instruments on Carnavale De Oriente (October 9). (Mela also has an album out this fall with Nicki Adams and Michael Eaton; Arrival is released on J-Man Records September 10, preceded by the title track.) AIRLFT‘s Spatial Recognition began as a monthly meeting, turned into a community and has now become an album (October 16). We’ll Let You Know When We Find Out, declare Sonelius Smith and Adam Kahan, mixing originals with standards by Monk, Beethoven and Gershwin (October 23). Gon Muruaga leads an international trio on Lines in the Sky, an extremely active recording overflowing with happy notes (October 28). On November 11 we’ll hear FRAGMENTS, from bassist and bandleader Bishu Chattopadhyay, followed a day later by Pat Thomas‘ playful Of all people…, preceded by the highly unusual and engaging “OOPS” (November 12).   Not to be outdone, Endectomorph Music has announced nine fall albums, taking us all the way through December. The fun begins with Christian Li‘s Broken Neon Sign, a mix of instrumental and vocal, improvised and composed (September 4). Then the attention turns to alto saxophonist Kevin Sun for I and II, which includes a cover of “Laura Palmer’s Theme” (September 25). Sunhyun Yoo‘s PLAiDE is filled with sax and decorated with synth and Moog (October 2). Next is the sextet Sundate on October 9, followed by pianist Dabin Ryu and friends on Discomfort. (November 6). Be sure to save room for Matei Predescu‘s Basmeon November 20, Joechen Rueckert’s New Quartet on How to Survive a Beheading (November 20) and Ocelot‘s II on December 4: a generous slate! The Travel Agency Is On Fire is one of the wildest releases of the season. The four-disc box set is a tribute to William S. Burroughs, billed as Anne Waldman, Thurston Moore, James Ilgenfritz, Anagram Ensemble but involving many other guest stars, from Bill Laswell to Tortoise. Fans of spoken word poetry and improv should order on the spot (Infrequent Seams, September 25).   Viola artist Jessica Pavone plays solo on half of …Is In the Air and collaborates on the other half, the best of both worlds (Relative Pitch/Weird Cry, October 16). Given the rather bland title Four Pieces for Viola and Sampler, one might expect the album to be a staid affair; quite the contrary. AJ Nilles & Tom Schneider are often raucous and always wild; you can’t judge an album by the title! (Macro, October 9). Avant cellist Topo Lyo offers quiet scenes from tokyo, embracing bass-like notes with tape loops while constructing humble tributes to nature (Faitiche, November 6). Out of Your Head Records launches autumn with The Realist, showcasing the work of cellist Janel Leppin (September 11). Then it will be time for Mali Obomsawin, the bassist and vocalist leading a nonet on the diverse Automatic (October 16). Next on the docket is acoustic bassist Stephan Crump, who leads a quartet on Passerine, inspired by the work of birds building their nests (October 23). Ambiances Magnétiques has two releases slated for September 25. Érick d’Orion‘s Mes fantômes is thick in some places, thin in others, so that one can hear the phantom threads. Super Scintillant‘s Tarot is jazzier, reflecting the interplay between bass clarinet and modular synthesizer, thanks to Mélanie Bourassa and Nicolas Bernier. Earshift is prepping two releases for September. Awakening is a collection of Armenian music, brought to life by the ensemble Visions of Nar (September 18), while trumpeter Tom Avgenicos leads a quartet on I’ll Go Where You Go as Delay 45, with an emphasis on dynamic contrast (September 25). A large part of Adam Rudolph‘s ensemble is from Türkiye, which results in some fascinating timbres of ney, cuika, waterphone and darbuka. Toys and found objects are also included. Invisible Threads is out on Northern Spy, September 18. Payton MacDonald leads marimba and percussion duos on Transients Vol. 1, 2, & 3, pairing with Susie Ibarra, Billy Martin and Nava Dunkelman (Infrequent Seams, September 4). Baritone saxophonist Tamar Osborn is set to release Varier: Berlin, the first of two albums to be recorded with separate ensembles. (Varier: London will follow next year.) The album is a celebration of the sights and sounds of the city, suffused with an underlying grief and eventual healing as the artist mourns the death of her father (October 2). Duologues 7: Distillation is the latest release from the saxophone and piano duo of Ivo Perelman and Matthew Shipp. Squidco is promising to release a new collaboration every year “in perpetuum” (October 2).   Blair / Huber‘s ECLIPSE is a thoughtful work for saxophone and guitar, the first of an extensive fall slate for LEITER; the rest is under wraps for now (October 16). Liba Villavecchia and Vasco Trilla (sax and drums) make a joyful noise on Serrat, with two side-long jams and album art that reflects the angular sound (defkaz, September 1). Sax and drums duo Nicole McCabe and Savannah Harris offer the warm and friendly All Together Now, prefaced by the single Lonely People, which makes them seem anything but (Sudden Quarterly, September 18). Likely the oldest performer in this article, trumpeter Wadada Leo Smith is still going strong at age 84. Constellations and Hemispheres finds the musician voyaging into inner and outer space with the help of four ensembles, a testament to his versatility (Burning Ambulance, September 25). Also released on Burning Ambulance, trumpeter Michael Sarian presents In This Desert, anchored by the three-part title track, redolent of heat shimmer and wide open spaces (September 25).   Images on loan is the first taste of Yuma Koda‘s enveloping Amid Kinos, which includes appearances from a variety of guest performers on instruments and spoken word. The tone is one of focused calm (Newhere Music, October 2). A similar feeling is created by pianist Kris Davis, leading the Kris Davis Trio on Lost in Geneva, which sounds like being pleasantly found (4166, September 25). Spoken word meets musique concrète on the ambitious Chinese Benefits, recorded on a failing iPhone 6 by A Large Sheet of Muscle (Drowned by Locals, October 16). Pianist Kevin Hays is Live at the Stone. Each of the four pieces includes a guest appearance, which lends the set great tonal variety. One title is “Bob Dylan” (AHT, September 13). Jamie Safir‘s Momentism is playful and warm, a jazzy excursion from a quartet whose sound pairs well with the name of the label (Chill Tone, September 4). A Mind in Motion is the first of Shifting Paradigm‘s fall releases, guitarist Zebu Zheng in charge of a quartet, sounding personal and upbeat (September 18). Following in its wake is Andrew Toombs‘ Alloy; we love the blue and purple cover, along with the laidback grooves (October 16). And we’re not sure how long it takes to make a cake look like a circuit board, but if that’s a photograph on the cover of Twin Talk‘s Delights, color us impressed (October 13). Vibraphonist Jalen Baker leads a nonet on RePaved, a breezy collection of tunes that honors the history of Houston TX’s 3rd, 4th and 5th Wards (Cellar Music, September 4). Bassist Emma Dayhuff leads a septet on Mountains, which seeks to translate the wonder of Montanan vistas into jazz (Division 81, September 4). An eleven-piece ensemble performs A World That Bears a Question, a 28-part suite inspired by Haruki Murakami’s novel 1Q84. One need not read the novel to understand the music of Madre Vaca, but we recommend doing both at once (September 18). Contemporary jazz sextet ONMO offers In Time and Spirit, which draws from myriad influences and “sits outside of jazz time” (Clonmell Jazz Social, October 16). The self-titled album from Oslo ensemble Power Chords is hythmic and percussive, as captured in lead single “Clumsy,” an ironic title as “serendipitous” might make a better description (Sonic Transmissions, October 30). Moon Inhabitants invite you to experience Canned Luna, an exuberant explosion of Norwegian jazz. A sense of fun permeates the record, which has an infectious energy (Sauajazz, September 4). Also hailing from Norway, Hans P. Kjorstad finds room for jazz, folk, rock, modern composition and more in the welcoming Inn. An intriguing quirk of the “miniature orchestra” ~ each of the track titles has three letters (Phantom Limb, September 18).   Hypergarden‘s self-titled debut is a series of freeform jams bordering on rock. Our favorite title is “Invasion of the Hydrangeas” (September 25). The improvising trio Lothar Ohlmeier / Isambard Khroustaliov / Rudi Fischerlehner unveils Landscapes on October 9, referencing both musique concrète and punk (Not Applicable). Mike Reed’s Separatist Party is rocking and rolling on Sing the Color Blue, another left turn from the always reliable Thrill Jockey (October 22). Between avant jazz and noise lies the raucous Evangelium, from Frode Gjerstad / Karl Bjorå / Håvard Skaset. The music tumbles, intertwines and roars (Conradsound, October 1). Eyes of Moon is a loud, romping jam from Tomchess, a multi-instrumentalist joined by a cavalcade of stars (Amalgam, September 15). The iconoclastic Ka Baird teams with Chris Ryan Williams to present Enthalpy. Onomatopoeic vocals are laid atop diagonal instrumentation, sounding like curious creatures from another world (Outside Time, September 25). Richard Allen

items.body: Daast Abyssal Highway self-released Manchester’s Daast hasn’t ever been easy listening, but even in comparison to their previous releases, new EP Abyssal Highway sounds gnarly. While there’s still snatches of techno-industrial in the mix, especially in the rolling rhythm underneath the title cut, the whole affair has been drenched in grit and saturated noise, delving deep into to death industrial territory. Its a sound that suits the project, which still manages to work some dark melodics into the fibres of the screeching death march of “Witch Thighs”, the brief moments of reprieve heralded by its pads quickly subsumed by waves of feedback and relentless, ugly percussion. Still, while it’s unlikely to light up the dancefloor of your local dance haven, there’s no denying how important those rhythms are to the Daast sound; closing cut “Unknown Regolith” strips far back to just its drums and some big drones halfway through, a switch to relative minimalism so effective to the point that even the addition of a slightly more fuzzed out layer of distortion to the snare becomes car crash impactful. It’s an EP of truly glorious, ugly sounds, unabashed, unyielding, and ever moving forward. Abyssal Highway EP by Daast Prophän Ana Lemlhi F Dnoubi (أنا الملهي فذنوبي) Antibody Moroccan producer Othman Cherradi’s move to Paris provided the thematic inspiration for new EP Ana Lemlhi F Dnoubi (أنا الملهي فذنوبي) but you don’t need to have that context or the ability to parse its Arabic lyrics to feel the restless, haunted mood which is woven through its combination of industrial beats, folk instrumentation, and downtempo by way of dark ambient production. There’s a classic blast furnace texture to opener “Habss Ezzaj” which should appeal to vintage Cold Meat Industry listeners, and on a more contemporary tip “Ana Lmalhi F Dnoubi” recalls Snakes Of Russia in how it gives its metallic strikes space to echo, and how it ameliorates their tactility with smokey ambiance. But when it eschews drum programming for the sake of more ambient pieces, Prophän loses none of his presence or menace. The funereal beauty of “Katssali Bhal Hakka”, which sets wistful vocals to organs and pads, carries the sound of much late era Coil towards a muted, inner, frailty.Ana Lmalhi F Dnoubi أنا الملهي فذنوبي by Prophän The post Observer: Daast & Prophän appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Primal Forms is quite a propulsive and beautifully elaborated electronic synthedelica effort that will ravish listeners of adventurous music with dancing, then hallucinogenic qualities. The synergy between the two musicians works like magic and with a clear easiness. A refreshing creative impulse to vintage analog electronic devices Primal Forms by Phantom Horse   Never heard about this project before, but as an avid listener/follower of the excellent Umor Rex‘s musical production, I wanted to give it a try. I must say I did right because this German duo embraces, in a very cool and inspiring way, the revival of Cosmic-electronic music in the pure tradition institutionalized by pioneering 70s sound artists such as Paul Baumann or Edgar Froese (Tangerine Dream), Bernd Kistenmacher, Mario Schönwalder, Software, Cosmic Hoffmann, Michael Hoenig et al, and a few materials reissued by the key label Bureau B. What makes this duo original and distinctive is that the two musicians, Ulf Schütte and Niklas Dommaschk, are capable of giving a second breath and a refreshing creative impulse to vintage analog electronic devices (notably modular synth technologies), thanks to hyper-efficient and trance-inducing minimal electronic pieces. Some tracks and their concise mechanical rhythms based on sequencers are reminiscent of a few synth-pop pioneering works. Globally, the compositions deliver an electro-pop ambient dimension enhanced by almost minimal-techno grooves and downtempo beats. Lysergic moments made of obsessional circular motifs and electronic oscillations are quite perceptible in the superb “Focus.” Some refined neo-psychedelic mantras made of vibrant droney chords, repetitive patterns, and melodious counterpoints will really transport the listener to another dimension. The compositions offer a lot of surprises, strangely experimental moments, and a blooming sense of electro-pop music dominated by catchy melodies. In a way, it operates a nice and welcoming synthesis between abstract synth experimentalism and more pulsating, groovy electronica. The album closes with the spacious, inter-sidereal, mellow, elastic, melodious-tinged, and utterly captivating “Umbra-Mechanik,” which closes the album in a brilliant manner. All in all, Primal Forms is quite a propulsive and beautifully elaborated electronic synthedelica effort that will ravish listeners of adventurous music with dancing, then hallucinogenic qualities. The synergy between the two musicians works like magic and with a clear easiness. Quite recommended for fans of neo-space music with a Berlin-style-oriented sound such as Zombi, Sankt Otten, Emeralds… but also more classical acts of the genre like Harmonia, Conrad Schnitzler, or Radio Massacre International. The album is delivered in a beautiful vinyl format, seconded by a digital version. Primal Forms is available on Umor Rex. [Bandcamp] Primal Forms by Phantom HorseThe post Phantom Horse :: Primal Forms (Umor Rex) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by kenfromlaisve — Cathedral ? Stained Glass Stories: A Masterclass MisunderstoodStained Glass Stories stands as one of the great lost artifacts of 1970s American independent music. Self-released in 1978 via Delta Records - a fiercely DIY operation situated above the Palace Theater in Times Square - this singular statement by New York's Cathedral remains one of my absolute favourite albums. It is a record that demands attention not just for what it is, but for what it firmly is not. There is a persistent, lazy critical shorthand that attempts to dismiss Cathedral as merely derivative of the British symphonic prog giants. As a longtime listener of both Genesis and Yes, I find these claims entirely baseless. If the band were simply tracing the outlines of their predecessors, the similarities would be glaringly obvious - yet they aren't there. How any reviewer can draw a line between this record and Genesis's Nursery Cryme is baffling; the two albums share zero overlap in texture, architecture, or intent. Cathedral wasn't mimicking the old guard; they were constructing their own highly complex, insular soundscapes from the ground up.The true anchor of this album - and a reason it is essential listening for any student of the instrument - is the sublime bass playing of Fred Callan. Often utilizing Moog bass pedals to widen the low-end spectrum, Callan's work weaves through the intricate arrangements with a commanding, lyrical presence. Nowhere is this more apparent than on my favourite track, 'Gong'. It is an absolute masterclass in instrumental tension, anchoring the band's most ambitious rhythmic ideas. Yet, to single out one track almost feels unfair to the cohesive brilliance of the pressing. The quality simply never subsides. From the sweeping, twelve-minute-plus opener 'Introspect' to the labyrinthine structural shifts of 'Days & Changes' and the closing epic 'The Search', the momentum never wavers. The band - rounded out by Tom Doncourt's expansive keyboard textures and Mercury Caronia IV's exhaustive percussion arsenal - managed to capture lightning in a bottle, tracking the material largely live to a sixteen-track Ampex machine. The only lingering downer surrounding Stained Glass Stories is its isolation in the archives. It is a profound pity that we do not have a more exhaustive canon of work from such a remarkable group. While the band eventually regrouped decades later to release a belated sophomore effort, 2007's The Bridge, one can only imagine the discography that might have materialized had they been afforded the runway they deserved during their initial run.

items.body: Of the many things that make albums featuring John Butcher unique, I believe the most outstanding characteristic is not that he likes to play at unusual venues (caves, water reservoirs, oil tanks…), but rather the fact that every ensemble he plays with is so diverse and incomparable that it allows the listener to hear many different facets of his playing. In an interview with Brad Rose, Butcher said that when improvising, he likes to hear the musician behind the instrument, though it’s not important to him to hear the musicians putting themselves in the spotlight - on the contrary, he tends to seek subtlety. In general, he looks for musicians who have already developed a personal musical style and their own way of playing - something that truly feels like their own. It is therefore almost inevitable that the various ensembles he selects based on these criteria will possess a unique dynamic and sonic world. One of last year’s best albums was RARE , John Butcher’s duo with French pianist Sophie Agnel, with whom he had been playing quite frequently over the last few years. I especially liked their improvisational rigor and the relaxed, varied, and aleatoric moments. On RARE , I considered the pauses in the music to be the central element; on foams & mesh , it’s different, mainly due to Pascal Niggenkemper (bass) and Ståle Liavik Solberg (drums), because the two of them fill those gaps. Solberg, with whom Butcher has played since 2015 in many kinds of combinations, permeates the improvisation with his bone-dry and at times almost esoteric style, for example when he uses extended materials (especially in the quiet passages of the first track). This is complemented by Agnel’s trills, which she plays from inside the piano. Butcher contributes very delicate bird calls here, while Niggenkemper subtly saws at the very low strings of his bass. It feels as though one is listening to the goings-on in the courtyard of a Tibetan monastery. This can be heard around the 20-mark of the first, significantly longer improvisation on foam & mesh. Such passages contrast with highly expressive moments, in which the rhythm section performs in a demanding and driving manner, but Butcher remains unflappable and employs his entire repertoire - guttural sounds, chirps, tremolos, circular breathing, serial/repetitive patterns, etc. - with casual ease. Only at the end of the track Agnel’s clusters and crescendos, Niggenkemper’s alienated drones and Solberg’s accentuated interceptions tempt him into vibrato-heavy phrases. The album was recorded at the artacts festival in St. Johann/Austria in 2024 and in the first part of the encore the musicians showcase extended playing techniques, with Niggenkemper and Agnel holding the improvisation together by a somber drone. Then the bass and piano shift imperceptibly into their normal registers, and the piece grows denser, builds in intensity, becoming louder and more concentrated - like a tornado - before dissolving perfectly. foam & mesh is an extraordinary album, the band is a superb match. They have played only three concerts so far and I think I’m not the only one who hopes that there will be more to come. foam & mesh is available as a CD and as a download. You can buy and listen to the album on the label’s website: https://sluchaj.bandcamp.com/album/foam-mesh foam & mesh by B:A:N:S BAND: Sophie Agnel / John Butcher / Pascal Niggenkemper / Ståle Liavik Solberg Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由萨克斯手约翰·布彻、钢琴家索菲·阿涅尔、低音提琴手帕斯卡尔·尼根肯珀和鼓手斯托尔·利亚维克·索尔伯格组成的四重奏在音乐节现场录制。乐评指出，与布彻其他组合不同，尼根肯珀和索尔伯格填补了音乐中的留白，使即兴充满骨感而近乎秘传的声响。宁静段落中，钢琴内部拨奏、萨克斯鸟鸣式颤音与低音提琴极低音区的轻锯声交织，营造出类似西藏寺院庭院的氛围；而激烈段落中，节奏组驱动推进，布彻则以喉音、啁啾、循环呼吸、序列重复等丰富技巧从容应对。结尾返场部分，音乐家们从扩展技法的阴沉持续音开始，逐渐向常规音区过渡，密度与强度不断攀升，最终如龙卷风般消散。整张专辑展现了自由即兴中静谧与爆发之间的动态平衡，以及四位乐手高度个人化的声音语言。录音于2024年奥地利艺术节完成，是当代自由爵士与前卫即兴的一次紧密协作。

items._cn_summary: 该专辑汇集了日本前卫艺术家水野修孝的电子音乐作品，其中核心曲目《怒りの日》是一首具象音乐作品，作曲家特别注明必须以大音量播放。乐评人记录了与团队用Tannoy音箱以接近100dB的爆音进行聆听的体验，称声音如同斩击，使人重新感受到声音作为波动的物理存在。作品并非为耳机聆听设计，而是需要通过大型扬声器让声波包裹身体，以全身感知其冲击力与空间质感。这张唱片呈现了日本前卫艺术在电子音乐领域的独特实践，将观念性的播放指示与极端声压体验结合，拓展了听众对声音物理性和音乐呈现方式的认知。

items.body: Label: Calligram Records, 2026 Personnel - Geof Bradfield: tenor and soprano saxophone, bass clarinet; Ben Goldberg: clarinet, contra alto clarinet; Myra Melford: piano; Dana Hall: drums. What a wonderful time I had listening to this fantastic bass-less quartet, whose powerful avant-garde jazz captivates from start to finish. Recorded live at Chicago’s legendary Green Mill, Open or Close gathers compositions from all four members—saxophonist Geof Bradfield, clarinetist Ben Goldberg, pianist Myra Melford, and drummer Dana Hall—who, having crossed musical paths before in several contexts, make a remarkable debut as a group here. Ornette Coleman’s “ Open or Close ” is the stunning opener, showcasing a memorable eight-note riff that gradually evolves into staccato activity resembling rhythmic shocks of vibrant color. Initially, Melford constructs melodies around that riff, with Hall’s percussive driving force as her sole support. Goldberg’s sinewy clarinet phrasing also prompts quick responses from the drummer and effective comping from Melford; then Bradfield offers an earthy, motivic solo packed with tension and release before the theme returns. Melford’s “ A Line With a Mind of Its Own ”, inspired by American painter and sculptor Cy Twombly, is built over an exquisite scale, patiently expressed as a chamber-jazz concerto with moderate snare-drum effervescence, accelerations, and mounting intensity. The pianist also contributes the adventurous “ The Kitchen ”. Goldberg also brings two contrasting yet extremely effective compositions: “ Study of the Blues ” is definitely not your standard model within the genre, but rather a slightly dissonant exploratory piece with a lot of interesting things going on; “ Three Ingredients ”, on the other hand, is a bop-inflected piece centered on an expeditious figure. Starting as a conversation between contra-alto and bass clarinets, the tune evolves into a sort of avant-garde ragtime. The groove-forward standouts are marvelous to witness, and they provide a setting in which each musician’s distinct personality emerges naturally. Bradfield’s “ No Brand ”, a dedication to South African pianist Abdullah Ibrahim, flows with a feel-good, six-beat contra-alto clarinet groove, hi-hat buoyancy, and melodic discernment fueled by the parallel motion created by soprano sax and piano. During Goldberg’s beautifully articulated statement, there is no disruption to the groove in the lower register as he and the pianist switch roles. By the end, Bradfield and Melford mirror each other in thrilling interplay. Another dedication to a South African musician, bassist Johnny Dyani, comes with “ Lonely Flowers ”, a piece Dyani wrote himself and first recorded in 1978. These African scents also bring a touch of Sun Ra’s exoticism into play, and I love Bradfield’s fierce improvisational spirit here on tenor. Brimming with creative ideas, Open or Close has no weak tracks, with each one evoking thoughtful moods and sonic stimulation. These four musicians reveal exceptional musical capabilities, and their collective effort comes highly recommended. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Open or Close ► 03 - No Brand ► 04 - Study of the Blues ► 06 - Lonely Flowers

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Emilio Gordoa与已故音乐家Sven-Åke Johansson的二重奏录音，呈现一种高度自觉的集体即兴创作。乐评强调其音乐如同平行线运动中浮现出的“第三层”，带有近乎神秘的幽灵特质。作品通过紧密的回声与共振，构建出类似萨蒂“家具音乐”的背景式声响，却并非退隐，而是增强意识、制造催眠般的接近狂喜的状态。两位演奏者之间的互动被描述为一种同时进行的倾听与书写，形成难以言说但具有转化力量的复杂重叠视野。专辑以45转LP发行，封面以德西双语呈现标题，并带有独特的排版设计。乐评认为这类音乐无法被严格分析或描述，其意义在聆听者与声音的协作中生成，既具透明性又不可捉摸，代表即兴互动边缘的持续探索。

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Ran Blake与Dominique Eade的钢琴与人声二重奏合作。Blake以其独有的方式将看似不相关的素材并置，比如将Max Roach的曲目与流行情歌、传统民谣与Michel Legrand的作品串联，他不是简单诠释，而是如同MRI扫描般揭示音乐内部的组织与关联，让熟悉的声音呈现出全新的样貌。Dominique Eade的演唱路径与Blake的长期搭档Jeanne Lee不同，她不以Billie Holiday式的根源为重心，也不倾向极简的克制表达，而是以饱满而深层的歌唱喜悦来塑造歌曲，这种特质从Whitney Houston的热门曲目一直延伸到Mingus的黑色风格作品，赋予整张专辑一种独特而亲切的感染力。乐评强调Blake多年来与歌手的合作是其核心脉络，而这张唱片则避开了早期经典作品的光环，展现了另一条值得关注的声乐与即兴钢琴交融的路径。

items.body: Celer has been at the forefront of ambient music for over a decade now, with an enormous discography spanning dozens of releases. Fellow American John Daniel has been making music as Forest Management for almost as long. Their new collaboration “Landmarks” takes inspiration from the book and film Mosquito Coast, the story of a man who abandons the American way of life for a remote coastal region of Honduras but becomes increasingly obsessed, with tragic consequences for him and his family. Snippets from both versions of the tale are heard at various points across the album, but the narrative is not spelled out and connections with the music mostly remain below the surface. As the opening soft, ethereal drone hovers at the edge of perception, you’d be forgiven for thinking you’d landed slap-bang in the middle of Celerland. From then on, however, the album takes several detours: birds sing tunefully in a loop over an echoing thud; distant thunder and clatter draws out a gurgling in the deep; grand, majestic melodic refrains are bathed in shimmering light. There are plenty of warm ambient drones to be heard, with indistinct, barely-there textures and endless repetition marking tracks such as ‘Indistinguishable from magic’ and ‘Volcanic institutions’. But there are also moments of greater resolve and certainty, as with the plodding drone of ‘Hotel Mona Lisa’, and unexpected twists and turns such as the faint echoes of previous drones in ‘S-shaped isthmus’. I found it impossible to tell which creative choices originated with which artist, such is the seamlessness with which their respective contributions are woven together. Ultimately I hear no judgement on Mosquito Coast‘s flawed would-be hero, even as his high-minded ideals lead him down a slippery slope of violence and obsession. The tumbling four-note refrain and singing high-pitched exclamation of the closing track ‘Rights of the idea or a machine’ could be interpreted equally easily as elegiac or as tragic. Either way, this is an album that, despite its frequent lushness, still manages to unsettle and provoke, as the best ambient drone music can. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以《蚊子海岸》的书影为灵感，但并未直述叙事，而是让故事线索隐没于声响底层。开篇的柔和飘渺长音延续了Celer标志性的氛围语法，随后逐渐偏离预期：鸟鸣循环与回声般的撞击并置，远雷与杂响引出深层咕噜声，庄严旋律沐浴在微光般的音色中。作品在温暖的环境 drones 与更具确定性的缓慢脉冲之间游走，如《Hotel Mona Lisa》呈现稳定的推进感，而《S-shaped isthmus》则让先前 drones 的残响以意外方式折返。两位艺术家的贡献被编织得难以分辨，整体听感高度统一。结尾曲目的坠跌式四音动机与高音呼喊在挽歌与悲剧之间保持暧昧，使唱片即便频繁展现丰茂质感，仍透出不安与挑衅性，体现了氛围 drone 音乐在沉浸之余制造疏离的潜力。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki以自制乐器演奏，将废弃物改造成音准精准的管弦与打击乐器，创造出独树一帜的声音世界。专辑延续前作的拼贴式风格，融合克莱兹默、昆比亚、非洲节拍与桑巴等多种世界音乐元素，并在每首曲目中展现即兴演奏的功力。乐评特别强调其乐器在录音话筒下仍保有丰富饱满的音质，同时旋律与节奏编排层次分明，既有传统韵味又不失实验趣味。无论是以单簧管模仿克莱兹默的欢腾，还是弗鲁特与拉丁打击乐交织的律动，都体现了乐队在跨界融合上的巧思。这张专辑不仅是手工乐器的展示，更以幽默而真挚的方式证明了音乐创造力不依赖昂贵的器材，而是源于对节奏、旋律与和声的普遍热爱。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: 挪威卡米拉·霍尔三重奏的新作《Langs》延续了他们对民间音乐的探索，但较前作更贴近地面。专辑以高音萨克斯为叙事核心，将挪威西部弹簧舞曲旋律与爵士即兴紧密结合。乐曲中角色界限被刻意模糊，贝斯手与萨克斯手齐奏旋律，模块合成器与电颤琴的叠录为整体增添色彩，节奏层也随之展开。随着推进，作品呈现出更强的即兴特质，传统旋律在开放结构中被反复拆解与重组。这种在民间素材、爵士语法与电子音色之间自由游走的方式，既保留了北欧民间音乐的文化底色，又赋予其当代实验性的表达空间。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa在Fazioli钢琴音乐厅进行两小时无脚本独奏即兴，随后在混音中加入稀疏的人声、打击乐、循环、田野录音与found sounds，形成一部兼具冥想气质与实验声景的作品。专辑源于疫情封锁、婚姻结束与米兰演出取消后的偶然邀约，在空旷音乐厅中一次成型的自然演奏被保留为“第一遍”的灵魂之声。Sosa强调避免风格标签，将爵士、拉丁、古典与传统元素以非线性方式重组，同时融入对灵性与人类处境的思考。其创作既延续了Monk式“绝不重复”的即兴精神，也通过钢琴内部拨弦、琴弦延音呼应等手法扩展了独奏的表现力。后期制作的稀疏点缀让纯钢琴的共鸣与现场环境音交织，呈现出一种扎根传统又走向未知的进化式艺术路径。

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以田野录音的方式，记录了芝加哥枪击暴力幸存者在街头巷尾的真实声音。制作人Ian Brennan未添加任何音乐，仅保留了现场的自由说唱、口述、环境噪音与社区日常背景声。二十五位参与者年龄从十七岁到六十七岁，大多来自同一个街区，几乎每个人都直接或间接受过暴力影响。录制当天恰逢特朗普下令向该市部署国民警卫队，地点位于社区领袖九十四岁祖母的门廊前，头顶是米德韦机场的航道。制作人发现，主动要求讲述的人反而平淡，而沉默迟疑者的讲述最令人动容；一位老人哽咽着反复道歉，因为她失去了两个儿子——真正该道歉的是社会。专辑收益捐给致力于以公共卫生方法终结暴力的Cure Violence Global。它不是传统意义上的音乐，而是让被遗忘社区以自己的声音直接在场的声音档案。

items.body: Review by Kayhan — Every now and then you come across an album that makes all the usual genre labels feel completelyuseless. For me, betcover!!'s UMA is easily one of the most interesting, downright fun and genuinelystrange records to come out of Japan in recent years. Trying to put a label on it feels prettypointless, if I had to describe it it's simply jazz-rock with no limits.The first thing that grabbed me was the emotional range across the tracklist. In one song you feellike you're losing your mind to frantic rhythms, loud brass and wild energy. Then unexpectedly thenoise drops away, and you hear this quiet, deeply sad melody that cuts straight to the heart. Veryfew bands can pull off that kind of contrast without sounding messy or broken.Importantly, none of the intricate parts feel like showing off for the sake of it. The jazz turns,the prog patterns and the odd experiments blend together so naturally that the music always feelsalive and unpredictable, never sterile.It packs intense energy, complex ideas and deep sadness all into a single spin. That balance isessentially why I love both prog and jazz in the first place. It's not about cold technicalperfection, but the thrill of unpredictability and the actual emotional weight behind every note.Also, do yourself a favor and check out their live performances if you get the chance. The songstake on a completely different life on stage and the raw energy makes the whole thing hit evenharder.
items._cn_summary: BETCOVER!! 的《UMA》是一张几乎无法归类的专辑，评论者将其描述为无界限的爵士摇滚。整张唱片在情绪跨度上极为丰富——前一刻还在以狂躁节奏、嘹亮铜管和失控能量让人精神错乱，下一刻却骤然安静下来，露出直击内心的悲伤旋律。专辑将爵士转调、前卫段落与各种奇特实验编织在一起，听感始终鲜活且不可预测，却毫无炫技感。作者强调其魅力在于将高强度能量、复杂构思与深层哀伤熔于一炉，平衡了前卫与爵士的核心吸引力。此外，乐队现场演出被特别提及——舞台赋予作品全新生命力，原始能量让冲击力倍增。整体来看，这是一张在融合与实验层面展现出强烈原创性的作品。

items.body: Every definition closes off certain possibilities. Naming an experience can help us understand it, but a name can also become a verdict, reducing a person to one fixed account of who they are and what their wounds mean. Human beings are rarely so easy to settle. We contradict ourselves, bear the consequences of our choices, and continue to change even after others believe they understand us. Resistance may begin there: in defending the right to remain complex, unresolved, and unfinished. Berlin post-punk and darkwave mainstays Golden Apes enter that unsettled territory with Resistance, the first single from The Sun Came Up Tremendously, their twelfth studio album, due September 18 through Icy Cold Records. Released today alongside a film written and directed by vocalist Peer Lebrecht, the song treats opposition as an internal friction: the force that keeps identity from hardening into a final shape, even when certainty would be easier. Resistance opens on a resonant guitar figure, answered by a single low keyboard tone. Hi-hats enter with a dry sizzle; Christian Lebrecht’s bass gives the piece forward pressure, while wavering synths and Salomon Bosse’s drums steadily enlarge the frame. Once the heavier guitar figure lands, the track assumes the emotional scale of mid-’80s gothic rock. Peer Lebrecht sings in a deep baritone that stays composed as the arrangement grows dense, and the guitars follow the cadence of his lines with a spring-loaded post-punk lift before thickening between verses. At intervals, the drums loosen into splashes, and the rhythm pulls back, leaving more air around Peer’s euphoric delivery. A clean, melodic guitar solo settles at the center point, almost plain in its design; its calm gives the vocal’s return greater weight. The measured bass, sober guitar tone, and baritone gravity recall Scottish cult band Lowlife, while the surrounding textures remain recognizably Golden Apes. The band describes the song’s central idea in terms of identity, complexity, and damage: “…Maybe that is the actual resistance. Not resistance against an external system, but resistance against final form. Against definition. Against the temptation to trade complexity for peace. Half-damaged instead of neatly resolved. I am the enemy…” Lebrecht’s film, based on a lucid dream by Vito Schneider, transfers that internal struggle to an abandoned clinical ward rendered in sickly greens and exhausted amber. A striped spinning top travels down an empty corridor; barefoot figures in hospital gowns occupy tiled rooms and enact private systems whose purpose never fully declares itself. One scrubs water from a floor into a bucket, another fills a bathtub, one drinks from a metal cup, and another holds an open umbrella beneath a dry ceiling. A solitary player moves grapes across a checkerboard, while a black telephone waits inside a star-lined suitcase. Elsewhere, a reel-to-reel machine runs beside clasped hands, as though recording testimony from a room that has forgotten its questions. Golden Apes perform throughout the ward, each member stationed apart in bathrooms, bare rooms, and passages. High overhead angles flatten bodies into diagrams, while the repetition of circular objects—the spinning top, fruit, reel hubs, and drum heads—turns the building into a machine for processing unresolved thought. In the closing coda, a black-clad figure carries armfuls of hospital gowns into a laundromat and feeds them into a washer. The garments pass through one more cycle, suggesting cleansing, erasure, recurrence, or all three at once. Watch the video for Resistance below: For more than two decades, Golden Apes have moved among post-punk, darkwave, gothic rock, indie rock, and electronic experiment, bringing delicate guitar melodies, driving bass, and Peer Lebrecht’s sonorous voice into a language of their own. The Berlin group has appeared at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Castle Party, and Murder of Crows, toured across Europe, the United States, Canada, and Russia, and shared stages with And Also The Trees, The Chameleons, Pink Turns Blue, Clan of Xymox, She Past Away, Whispering Sons, TRAITRS, Then Comes Silence, and A Projection. The Sun Came Up Tremendously follows the band’s 2024 album Our Ashes at the End of the Day. Its ten songs were written between 2024 and 2025, then recorded and produced at Thommy Hein Studios in Berlin from late 2025 into early 2026. Resistance was mixed by Thommy Hein and Peer Lebrecht and mastered by Hein, who also contributes guest guitar. The current Golden Apes lineup comprises Peer Lebrecht on vocals and synths, Maximilian Hennig and Stephan Schönefeld on guitars, Christian Lebrecht on bass, and Salomon Bosse on drums. “…o sun, that healest all distempered vision, thou dost content me so, when thou resolvest, that doubting pleases me no less than knowing!” – Dante Alighieri, Divina Commedia Listen to Resistance below, and pre-order The Sun Came Up Tremendously through Bandcamp. The album arrives September 18 via Icy Cold Records. items._cn_summary: 柏林后朋克老牌乐团推出新单曲《抵抗》，选自九月发行的第十二张录音室专辑。歌曲将抵抗诠释为个体对自身复杂性、未完成状态的坚持，拒绝被定义或固化。编曲以回响吉他乐句与低音键盘起笔，踩镲带着干涩质感切入，贝斯驱动节奏，合成器与鼓组逐步扩展声场。主唱低沉男中音在厚重织体中保持镇定，吉他随唱词起伏，并在段落间强化厚度。中段一段简洁旋律独奏令整体暂时松弛，为歌者回到麦克风前蓄积更大份量。乐评认为沉稳贝斯与肃穆吉他音色令人想起苏格兰邪典乐队，但环绕氛围仍保持乐团自身特征。同日发布的影片由主唱执导，灵感来自一个清晰梦境，场景设在废弃临床病房，患者赤脚进行擦地、接水、持伞、下棋等无明确目的的仪式，以超现实画面呼应歌词中‘半受损’的自我，将内在抵抗化为可视的私密剧场。
